source.title: Scaling Laws for Neural-Network Quantum States
source.authors: Riccardo Rende; A. Sinibaldi; Luciano Loris Viteritti; R. Wiersema; Antoine Georges; Giuseppe Carleo

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Extends the scaling-law question to transformer neural-network quantum states for quantum many-body ground-state optimization and reports its own scaling results.
record.gate_note: The paper measures V-score against training compute for four Hamiltonians and reports architectural and high-compute comparisons. The language-model scaling laws cited in the introduction are background, not this paper's results.
record.test_reason: The paper fits its own power law of a loss-like accuracy measure (V-score) against training FLOPs for transformer neural-network quantum states. This is a new training regime: variational ground-state optimization, not text pretraining. Its results bear on whether the power-law form carries over (V5) and on bending away from a single power law at high compute (V7).
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that the transformer NQS V-score decays as a power law in training compute for four 2D spin Hamiltonians. Rescaling collapses system sizes onto one curve with α ≈ β (size consistency), which they say allows compute estimates for larger systems. They find α decreases with frustration, making it a complexity measure. They report α robust to architecture and optimization details, which affect only the prefactor. Saturation at high depth, attributed mainly to the optimizer, limits the regime.
record.recipe_differences: Applies a power-law scaling analysis to transformer variational quantum states, using V-score and training FLOPs rather than language-model held-out cross-entropy, parameter/token sweeps, or compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The exponent is reported as robust to the tested patch-size and symmetry variants and to the tested sample-size change in the scaling regime. The high-compute saturation appears for both tested Monte Carlo sample sizes. Architecture and optimization choices can change the prefactor and V-score.

fits_no_version.finding: The fitted exponent α stays the same under patch-size change, symmetry projection and a change in Monte Carlo sample size. Only the prefactor A changes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scaling exponents are invariant to architecture details, which shift only the prefactor.

fits_no_version.finding: The exponent α falls systematically with frustration: 1.29 (square Heisenberg) to 0.40 (triangular J1-J2). α ≈ β, giving size-independent scaling.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The scaling exponent depends on the target task or data distribution and measures its difficulty.

record.problems: Evidence is limited to four Hamiltonians, system sizes L = 12, 16, 18, 20, and the tested transformer setup. The authors report saturation beyond nl = 12, so the power law does not hold throughout the largest-compute regime. Error estimates use the two best runs out of three seeds; numeric values for the architecture comparison and saturation plots are not tabulated.

untested.parts: Image and video models, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer, and other modalities are not tested. Power-law behaviour over several orders of magnitude is not shown: compute spans about one decade. Scaling with parameters or data separately is not tested.
Effects of parameter counting, training schedule, data and fitting method on the exponents are not tested. Disagreements over the compute-optimal split are not tested.
The authors claim the exponent lets compute for larger system sizes be estimated from smaller ones. They report no held-out validation that small-compute fits predict much larger runs.

record.verdict_notes: The V-score is a variance-based accuracy measure, not cross-entropy, and compute counts only forward-pass FLOPs. Compute is varied only by depth (nl 2–8 in the main fits). Each reported point is the best of three seeds, with the error taken as the spread of the top two. This selection may bias the fits. The exponent-invariance results were moved from V7 to fits_no_version because architecture is not a fitting or setup choice that V7 names. V4 is not tested: there is no fixed-parameter shape comparison.

versions.untested_parts: The paper studies V-score for quantum states, not held-out language-model cross-entropy or its scaling with parameter count and tokens.
The authors say smaller-system simulations can estimate compute for larger systems, but do not report a validation in which fits to small runs predict runs orders of magnitude larger.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep between model parameters and training tokens is reported.
Architectural variants are compared for scaling behavior, but the paper does not test loss differences at fixed parameter count across depth, width and other architecture details.

Tests transformer variational ground-state optimization for four spin Hamiltonians. It does not test image/video models, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, transfer, or other modalities and regimes.

Tests exponent robustness to selected architecture and optimization variations, and reports high-compute saturation. It does not test parameter-counting or fitting-method choices, data variation, or compute-optimal allocation disagreements.

rows.subject: Square Heisenberg (J2 /J1 = 0)
rows.operation_detail: Fit V-score to the scaling form V-score = A f^−α N^β and collapse data across system sizes.
rows.measure: V-score as a function of training compute; fitted power-law exponents and prefactor
rows.uncertainty: Table I reports α = 1.29(2), β = 1.31(3), log A = 16.5(5); errors estimated by resampling with Gaussian noise.
rows.locator: Section III, Fig. 1 and Table I
rows.note: The fit aggregates results across the stated system sizes; the paper reports collapse onto a power law.
rows.check: Link and state are correct. The fit spans only about one order of magnitude of rescaled compute (roughly 1 to 15 ×10^8 in Fig. 1), so 'over several orders of magnitude' is not established.

rows.subject: Transformer wave function, b = 2
rows.operation_detail: Compare the power-law scaling curve for patch size b = 2 with the b = 4 architecture.
rows.measure: V-score versus rescaled compute and scaling behavior across architecture variants
rows.baseline: b = 4 architecture; exact value not stated
rows.value: The text reports that the scaling behavior is unchanged and the exponent is the same as in Table I; the V-score is reduced and FLOPs increase. Exact values are figure only.
rows.note: The paper says architecture changes leave the exponent essentially invariant; this is evidence against exponent dependence on this tested architecture choice, not a fixed-parameter-count comparison.
rows.check: The V7 link should be removed. The comparison varies patch size, which is not one of the setup or fitting choices V7 names (parameter counting, schedule, data, fitting method). The 'absent' state was framed against V7. For V5, the b=2 data lie on the power law, so the state is observed. The paper reuses the Table I exponents rather than refitting, at L=12 only.

rows.operation_detail: Compare the power-law scaling curve for a b = 2 wave function augmented with translation symmetries against the b = 4 architecture.
rows.measure: V-score versus rescaled compute and scaling behavior across architecture variants
rows.baseline: b = 4 architecture; exact value not stated
rows.value: The text reports that the scaling behavior is unchanged and the exponent is the same as in Table I; the V-score is reduced and FLOPs increase. Exact values are figure only.
rows.note: The paper says architecture changes leave the exponent essentially invariant; this is evidence against exponent dependence on this tested architecture choice, not a fixed-parameter-count comparison.
rows.check: Same as R5. The V7 link should be removed and the state set to observed for V5. The paper does not refit the exponent; it says the data lie on the Table I fit.

rows.subject: Transformer wave function
rows.operation_detail: Extend the layer-count sweep to architectures with more layers and measure V-score against compute.

conditions.value: up to nl = 20; saturation beyond nl = 12

rows.measure: V-score as a function of training compute; departure from the power-law regime
rows.baseline: Power-law behavior in the lower-compute regime
rows.value: V-score begins to saturate beyond nl = 12; the paper says the scaling laws no longer apply in this large-compute regime.
rows.note: The text explicitly reports saturation; the plotted numerical values are not tabulated.
rows.check: V5 should be added. Saturation beyond nl=12 bounds the regime where the power law holds. For V7, the state observed means bending is observed. The authors attribute the saturation mainly to the optimizer, not to an intrinsic limit.

rows.subject: Transformer wave function
rows.operation_detail: Repeat the layer-count sweep with a larger number of Monte Carlo samples and measure V-score against compute.

conditions.value: up to nl = 20; saturation beyond nl = 12

rows.measure: V-score as a function of training compute; departure from the power-law regime
rows.baseline: Power-law behavior in the lower-compute regime
rows.value: The same large-compute saturation is reported beyond nl = 12; in the scaling regime, the curve has the same exponent as for M = 16 384.
rows.note: The authors say saturation at high compute for both sample sizes suggests it is not primarily controlled by sampling.
rows.check: V5 should be added, as for R7. The sample-size comparison shows the same exponent in the scaling regime and the same saturation at high compute.

relationships.condition: Transformer NQS ground-state optimization on four 2D spin Hamiltonians, L=12–20, within the lower-compute regime (nl ≤ 12)
relationships.reason: V-score follows A f^-α N^β with collapse across system sizes (α 0.40–1.29) (R1–R4). Patch-size and symmetry variants lie on the same fit (R5, R6).
relationships.display_finding: V-score followed A f^-α N^β with α=0.40–1.29 and collapse across system sizes, while patch-size and symmetry variants followed the same fit.

relationships.condition: Square J1-J2, L=12, deeper models (nl > 12, up to 20); whole study's compute range
relationships.reason: V-score saturates beyond nl=12 for both Monte Carlo sample sizes, so the power law fails at high compute (R7, R8). The fitted range covers only about one decade of compute.
relationships.display_finding: V-score saturated beyond 12 layers for both Monte Carlo sample sizes, breaking high-compute power-law improvement within a fitted range of about one compute decade.

relationships.condition: Square J1-J2, L=12, high-compute regime for M=16384 and M=20480
relationships.reason: The curves bend away from the single power law into saturation beyond nl=12 (R7, R8). The authors attribute this to optimization difficulty.
relationships.display_finding: Both curves saturated beyond n_l=12, departing from a single power law, which the authors attributed to optimization difficulty.
